analysis.one_liner: Extended patent-like monopolies on certain drugs and biologics in exchange for tied diagnostic tests.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given brand-name drug and biologic makers extra monopoly time — 6 to 12 more months of exclusivity when a company developed a companion diagnostic test, and 15 years of protection for so-called 'dormant therapies' for unmet medical needs, including patent extensions to fill any gaps. It also would have set up a more open process for Medicare to set payment rates for new lab tests, with an advisory panel of patients, clinicians, and experts. The aim was to encourage drugs tailored to diagnostic tests and treatments abandoned for weak patent protection, but the mechanism was longer monopolies, which keep lower-priced generic and biosimilar copies off the market longer.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug and biologic manufacturers that develop companion diagnostic tests would gain 6 to 12 additional months of market exclusivity, on top of existing exclusivity and any pediatric exclusivity [S2][S3]. Companies whose drugs qualify as 'dormant therapies' would get 15 years of data exclusivity — during which the FDA could not approve generic copies or biosimilars that rely on the original approval — plus automatic patent term extensions so patents last through the full 15 years [S2][S3]. Clinical laboratories would gain from a more structured, advisory-panel-based process for setting Medicare payment rates for new tests, with rates informed in part by private insurance payments [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers of drugs or biologics tied to a companion diagnostic test would get their existing exclusivity periods extended by 12 months (if the test was developed alongside the drug) or 6 months otherwise, and this stacks on top of pediatric exclusivity [S2][S3].

Drugs designated 'dormant therapies' for unmet medical needs would receive 15 years of data exclusivity, during which the Secretary could not approve generic (505(j)), follow-on (505(b)(2)), or biosimilar (351(k)) applications relying on the original approval; sponsors must waive enforcement of their listed patents after the period ends [S2][S3].
Patents on dormant therapies would be extended so they expire no earlier than the end of the 15-year protection period [S3].

Medicare's process for setting payment rates for brand-new clinical lab tests would gain defined factors and a 19-member independent advisory panel including patients, clinicians, and technical experts, with public meetings and comment [S3].
A new Advanced Diagnostics Education Council at HHS would publish standard terms and definitions for innovative diagnostics for patients, doctors, payers, and policymakers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients, private insurers, and Medicare would bear higher drug costs while the extended monopolies delay generic and biosimilar competition; generic and biosimilar makers would be barred from relying on the original approvals during the new exclusivity windows. Medicare would pay whatever rates the new gap-filling process sets for new lab tests, with private insurance rates as one input [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The central mechanism is longer monopoly: a 15-year data exclusivity period would block generic, follow-on, and biosimilar applications that rely on the original approval for a decade and a half, delaying lower-priced competition [S2][S3].

The extra 6-to-12-month exclusivity for drugs with companion diagnostics comes on top of existing exclusivity and pediatric exclusivity, and can apply twice to the same product, extending the period during which only the brand-name version is available [S3].

For Medicare's new-test rate setting, the bill would direct the Secretary to consider private insurance rates and laboratory charges, which tends to push government payment rates upward for new tests [S3].

The 'dormant therapy' and diagnostic-extension determinations are made at the sponsor's request, so the added exclusivity flows to whichever products companies choose to route through these pathways, not necessarily the ones with the greatest public health value [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real transparency improvements for Medicare lab-test rate setting and a genuine intellectual-property trade-off for dormant therapies (15 years of exclusivity in exchange for a post-period patent waiver). But its main lever for stimulating development was extending monopolies — and in the case of companion-diagnostic extensions, simply adding months to existing exclusivity with no reciprocal concession. The clearest cost falls on anyone paying for drugs: patients, employers, and Medicare, who would wait longer for cheaper generic and biosimilar versions. Weighing industry-focused incentives of this size against modest procedural gains, the costs to drug payers outweighed the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, referred to subcommittees, and never received any vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Leonard Lance introduced the bill on November 18, 2011 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees, and it was referred to the Health and Intellectual Property subcommittees [S5].
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it; it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients, insurers, and Medicare avoided the longer drug monopolies the bill would have created, and generic and biosimilar competition was preserved. The bill's ideas later resurfaced in the 2013-2014 MODDERN Cures reintroductions, but the diagnostics provisions were eventually folded into broader FDA legislation while the dormant-therapy exclusivity never became law.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split: of 48 cosponsors, 23 were Republicans and 25 were Democrats, with a Republican sponsor [S4].

industries.note: The bill would hand makers of drugs paired with diagnostic tests 6 to 12 extra months of exclusivity and give 'dormant therapies' 15 years of data exclusivity plus patent extensions — all of which delays generic and biosimilar competition and keeps drug prices higher for patients and payers [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Clinical diagnostic laboratories and test developers
industries.note: Labs and test developers would gain clearer, more predictable Medicare payment-setting for new tests, with private insurance rates as an input — which can raise Medicare costs — while a new education council would standardize diagnostic terminology [S2][S3].

During the new exclusivity windows the FDA could not approve generics, follow-on products, or biosimilars that rely on the original approvals, cutting these makers off from the affected markets for years [S3].
